I thank the representative of Ukraine for his statements and I will now give the floor to Ms. Claudia Fuentes Julio, Assistant Secretary General for Human Rights.

Thank you, Ambassador. Excellencies, dear co-sponsors, distinguished participants, I want to thank you for this opportunity to brief Council members and member states. Since 2014, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has maintained a presence in Ukraine through the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission. Every day, my colleagues engage with victims and witnesses, conduct site visits where access is provided, and undertake other work to verify alleged violation of international human rights law and humanitarian law, regardless of perpetrator. Over the first six months of this year, they verified a 37% increase in civilian casualties as compared to last year. the result of increasing strikes against populated areas and large-scale use of drones along the frontlines. This deadly pattern has continued into July and August, prompting the United Nations Secretary-General to call for urgent de-escalation. Today, we hold in our thoughts those killed and injured. along with their families, as well as those in detention or captivity because of this war. Exchanges of prisoners of war are ongoing between the Russian Federation and Ukraine. This is welcome. However, in the interim, OHCHR's monitoring shows that widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees by the Russian Federation authorities continues. This includes sexual violence. OSCHR has also continued to document torture and ill treatment of Russian and third country national prisoners of war in Ukrainian custody, albeit on a fundamentally different scale. OSCHR's assessment of the situation is based on extensive and comprehensive monitoring in line with our well-established methodology. Since February 2022, our staff has conducted 2,129 confidential interviews with prisoners of war and civilian detainees. This includes 910 interviews with Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees following their release from Russian captivity, as well as 816 Russian and 57 third country national prisoners of war while interned in official facilities in government-controlled territory of Ukraine, where OHCHR has regular and unimpeded access. OHCHR continues to urge the Russian Federation to provide access to facilities in occupied territory of Ukraine and in the Russian Federation. Excellencies, Since February 2022, OHCHR has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the death of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody resulting from torture, denial of medical care or other inhumane conditions of detention. More than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed by our office reported having experienced torture or ill treatment during captivity, often repeatedly over prolonged periods. More than half also reported sexual violence. We receive consistent account of severe beatings with objects such as batons, heavy belts and wood, electric shocks, dog attacks, mock executions, and other forms of torture. Forms of sexual violence documented include rape, gang rape, beating while nude, beatings to the genitals, electric shocks to the genitals and ******* and degrading treatment of a sexualized nature. Those interviewed consistently described conditions of detention across facilities operated by the Russian Federation as inhumane and marked by severe deprivation of basic necessities. Released prisoners of war refers to chronic food deprivation, food deliberately contaminated with insects and other objects, inadequate clothing, prolonged exposure to cold, lack of basic hygiene, very limited medical care that led to the spread of infectious diseases, including tuberculosis and skin diseases causing painful wounds, and near total isolation from the outside world. Interviewees indicate that such conditions were compounded by harsh detention regimes, seemingly replicated across multiple facilities. These included prolonged forced standing, forced physical exertion, sleep deprivation, constant surveillance, severe restrictions of movement and communication with the outside world, and severe physical punishment for minor infractions. creating an environment of continuous and extreme physical and psychological abuse. OHCHR does not have information about the number or condition of third country nationals who serve in the Ukrainian armed forces and are currently interned by the Russian Federation. With respect to Russian prisoners of war and third country nationals held by Ukraine interviewed by OHCHR since February 2022, Approximately half reported torture or ill treatment, primarily during the initial stage of captivity and interrogation and capture at unofficial places of detention. Our monitoring indicates that once these individuals arrive in official places of internment, the conditionals generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022. The situation of third country nationals held by Ukraine requires a specific consideration. These men, who were members of the Russian armed forces, not mercenaries, come from over 45 countries and face uncertainties about the future. Some have fears about what will happen if they return to the Russian Federation, while others fear returning to their country of origins where they may face criminal charges for fighting on behalf of another country. Many told us they have not intended to become soldiers, but were misled by deceptive recruitment practices. Excellencies, turning now to Ukrainian civilian detainees held by the Russian Federation after having been taken into custody in occupied territory. OHCHR conducts interviews with civilian detainees only after they have been released and reached places of safety, since the Russian Federation has not granted OHCHR access to places of detention. It is estimated that more than 16,000 civilians remain deprived of their liberty. OHCHR has found that many were detained arbitrarily and are held incommunicado under legal frameworks that do not comply with international law. Former civilian detainees held by the Russian Federation reported being subjected to the same patterns of abuse documented for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 85% of civilian detainees interviewed reported torture and ill-treatment, including sexual violence, while conditions of detentions were frequently inhumane, marked by food deprivation, inadequate medical services, and overall deplorable conditions of detention. We are particularly concerned that women detainees and prisoners of war reported similar abusive conditions. At least two pregnant women suffered a miscarriage following physical violence. In addition, the conditions were compounded by threats of sexual violence during interrogations, as well as gender-specific deprivations and degraded treatment. This included lack of menstrual health products in detention, invasive searches of bodily cavities, and forced nudity under the gaze of male guards and prisoners. Some women described being forced to be naked while menstruating as particularly humiliating. These gender-specific abuses intensify the women's sense of degradation, leaving them with a profound sense of vulnerability. Excellencies, looking forward, allow me to share some reflections on the challenges ahead and the steps needed to address them. Our office has established a comprehensive factual record of the treatment of prisoners of war and civilian detainees. and conditions of detentions in both the Russian Federation and Ukraine. We have documented violations, clarified the applicable legal frameworks, and provided detailed recommendations to end violation, strengthen protection, and inform future action. This work will continue. The challenge now is not simply to continue documenting what happens during detention. but to ensure that all those detained, both civilian and prisoners of war, are released safely and lawfully. Member States should begin preparing now for the challenges that will accompany any future political processes. This includes practical arrangements for the release, repatriation and safe return of civilians unlawfully detained by the Russian Federation, taking into account humanitarian considerations such the situation of pregnant woman, the wounded and sick, older persons, and those who have been detained for a long time. Arrangement should be made for the release by both the Russian Federation and Ukraine of prisoners of war, including the urgent release of those who are wounded, seriously ill, or have endured prolonged captivity, followed by an all-for-all exchange. It extends to separate consideration of third country nationals held by both Ukraine and the Russian Federation, including protection against refoulement where relevant, and post-release protection, rehabilitation, and family reunification for all prisoners of war. These are not issues that can be left until ceasefire or wider political settlement is reached. They require consideration now, including by many member states whose nationals are affected. OSTHR does not prescribe the political arrangement through which these issues should be resolved. We are ready to support the international community to identify procedural safeguards to ensure that arrangements are grounded international human rights, human rights, humanitarian law, provide independent monitoring and offer legal and technical advice. Collectively, we can ensure that protection of all prisoners of war and civilian detainees is not treated as an afterthought, but as an integral part of the ceasefire and political settlement process that is so desperately needed. With so many in detention for so long and enduring mistreatment, It is an imperative to join efforts now to secure their release. Thank you.

Thank you. Distinguished and honorable delegates, it's an honor to be here today to talk about our findings from our BBCI investigation, Putin's Foreign Fighters. I want to start by talking about how we came across the story. So in May 2024, my team and I began receiving voice notes from a group of young Syrian men on the front lines in Ukraine. They said they had been offered backline non-combat work in the Russian army, but instead found themselves on the front line of a war they knew nothing about. This was the start of our investigation, our year-long investigation into how Russia recruits foreign men into its ranks, tracing the recruitment pipelines from the Middle East, Asia, Central Africa, and beyond to the front line. We identified recruiters from different countries, but our investigation centred on one key person in Russia, Polina Alexandrovna Azarny, the woman responsible for recruiting these Syrian men we were speaking to. So Polina is a businesswoman and former teacher from Russia. And before the war, she was running a kind of account helping foreign students, often Arab young men, join Russian universities. So she would help them with their visas, their transport, et cetera. And this is a platform she later repurposed for recruitment where she started posting adverts to join the Russian army. And this is exactly how the Syrian group found Polina through these platforms. So what they were offered, as we are told, is a one-year contract with the Russian army, Russian citizenship, $2,500 a month, and a signing bonus of $5,000. And Polina told them that if they paid her a $3,000 cut, they would not be fighting on the front lines and doing non-combat support roles. However, over the course of our year-long investigation, we found that what happened was, in fact, different. Recruits received as little as 10 days of training before being deployed to the front lines. Military contracts were issued in Russian, a language most of the recruits didn't understand or speak. And most of them weren't able to leave after a year due to a decree that meant their contracts were automatically renewed, so they were not kept to their promises again. So after these findings, we started investigating the scale of Polina's operations. We found that her Telegram channel grew from 4,000 followers to 21,000 followers. And we identified nearly 500 cases where men were issued invitations to come to Russia and join the Russian army, mainly from Syria, Egypt, Yemen, Morocco, but also across Asia and Central Africa. and only today Polina posted a further 35 names who signed up for recruitment so this goes to show it is still ongoing. We also identified 12 families who told us their sons had died after Polina had recruited them to join the Russian army. And another thing we found by speaking to families was that Polina targeted very vulnerable student communities who were desperate for money. They told us their sons were struggling to pay their university fees, they were really struggling financially and Polina offered them a helpline. But I think what's also important to mention that Polina is one in a much larger transnational recruitment network. And we found that there are very different layers of recruitment. So one is what we just talked about, which is the online scouting on Telegram channels and social media platforms. So we found two other Telegram accounts in Arabic making similar offers to Polina. And our BBC India team also traced a blogger who was making similar and then there's also local smaller scale recruiters so we identified a local Syrian broker who was tapping into more local Syrian networks through WhatsApp and working with middlemen in Russia by sending them there and then also local but larger scale companies so we found a company in Oman who were offering hospitality and security jobs to men but in fact sending them to the Russian army and according to local lawyers over 400 men from Yemen were sent to Russia this way. And they confirmed to us that at least 24 of them had died. And in our journey of tracing these men, we also found that two of them had in fact been reported as dead to their families, but ended up in a prisoner of war facility in Ukraine. So when we also visited this prisoner camp, prisoner of war facility, we saw men from all over the world, Senegal, Sri Lanka, Egypt. And until this day, we're still receiving messages from families all over the world who are asking us to help find their sons. Greece remains deeply concerned by the mounting body of credible evidence verifying grave violations committed by the Russian armed forces against Ukrainian military personnel and civilians, as well as against foreign nationals. Successive reports by the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine and other credible organizations continue to document patterns of systematic torture, cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment, sexual violence, denial of adequate medical care and deaths in captivity. The latest report documents 129 summary executions of captured Ukrainian military personnel since February 2022, while nearly all of the released Ukrainian prisoners of war reporting torture or other forms of ill treatment. Equally alarming are the findings concerning arbitrary detention of civilians in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, and forced disappearances and transfers of protected persons into the territory of the Russian Federation. According to this year's Secretary General conflict related sexual violence report and reports of the UN Human Rights Office, hundreds of men and women in service but also civilian detainees and civilians in residential areas have been subjected to sexual violence. Ukrainian combatants are denied prisoner of war status, while civilian detainees are denied the right to a fair trial, including the principles of presumption of innocence and non-retroactivity of laws, as well as the right to be tried by an independent and impartial tribunal. Illegal Russian courts in the occupied territories apply Russian criminal law, contrary to Russia's own international obligations, as an occupying power. Many detainees are deported to Russia and tried before military courts, which is a war crime. All these practices constitute serious violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. International humanitarian law in this case, the third and fourth Geneva Conventions, establish clear obligations that are not optional or reciprocal. They apply in all circumstances and must be respected by all parties. Greece is also deeply concerned by reports concerning the recruitment of foreign nationals from at least 17 countries into the Russian army. Madam Chair, We call on Russia to abstain from further violations of international law, to ensure humane treatment of all prisoners of war and civilian detainees, grant unhindered access to independent international monitors, release unlawfully detained civilians, and hold those responsible accountable for their actions. In this regard, we take note of the readiness of competent Ukrainian authorities to conduct investigations, take action against human rights violations attributed to them and improve detention conditions. In conclusion, Madam Chair, respect for human dignity is a legal obligation and a moral imperative. Greece fully subscribes to national and international efforts to ensure accountability for all violations perpetrated during this war and bring those responsible to justice. In this context, we fully support the work of relevant international judicial mechanisms. We firmly believe that only by upholding international law and the principles of the UN Charter will we ensure a just and lasting peace in Ukraine and that it is essential that the issue of the humane treatment of POWs and civilian detainees is included in any peace talks. I thank you.

They reflect minimum standards of human treatment that must be guaranteed in all circumstances and across all territories. The DRC reaffirms its commitment to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their 1977 and 2005 Additional Protocols. The protection of human dignity cannot be subordinated to political, military or geographical considerations. While the prospects of a rapid solution to the conflict remain uncertain, the DRC remains deeply concerned by the continued hostilities and their human, political and security consequences. Indeed, every additional day of war brings with it its share of victims, it exacerbates the suffering of the civilian population, it worsens international divisions and poses a consistent threat to the maintenance of international peace and security. In line with its Consistent position within the Security Council, my country remains convinced that there can be no military solution to this crisis. The longer the conflict goes on, the prospects for a lasting solution diminish. Chair. My country's government feels that it is particularly important for today's debate to not further polarize positions. My delegation would like to underscore that the protection of civilian detainees, prisoners of war and humanitarian access must be at the heart of any international response. In that regard, the conditions must be created for humanitarian workers to be able to fully do their job in accordance with international humanitarian law. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their additional protocols remain the universal basis for the protection of persons that are not participating in or no longer participating in hostilities. Prisoners of war and civilian detainees, as well as all persons out of combat, must be treated with humanity and dignity, regardless of the circumstances of the conflict. No violation of international humanitarian law can be contextualized. Any violation deserves to be considered with incredible, impartial, and independent mechanisms so that the facts can be established and that who is responsible can be determined in accordance with international law. It is in the light of these principles that the question of prisoners of war, civilian detainees and foreign fighters is of particular importance today. Beyond its strictly humanitarian dimension, it is an indicator of the parties' capacity to preserve spaces for dialogue and to maintain channels of communication, without which no credible political prospect can emerge. Madam President, the DRC welcomes the exchange of prisoners that have taken place between the parties in recent months. These initiatives show that, despite the ongoing fighting, progress remains possible when humanitarian imperatives prevail. It also shows that dialogue is never entirely broken, even within the most testing conflicts. It is precisely this ability to achieve individual, one-off agreements that the international community should encourage in order to have a more substantial impact on the path towards peace. Madam Chair, the issue of foreign is also a cause of concern. Contemporary conflicts go beyond the borders of the states that are directly involved and affect the nationals of third countries, including African countries, that may find themselves involved, captured or trapped in hostilities in various different circumstances, sometimes due to their economic vulnerability or deceitful promises. Their protection, identification, the effective exercise of consular assistance, as well as as, of course, when circumstances allow, their repatriation must be the subject of strengthened cooperation among the parties concerned, states of origin and the relevant humanitarian organisations. The Democratic Republic of the Congo believes that this cooperation is also a tangible way to prevent the exploitation of vulnerable persons and to limit the internationalisation of this conflict. Madam Chair, respect for international humanitarian law is a legal obligation, it also represents an investment in peace. Every prisoner exchanged, every family reunited, every person found and every humanitarian measure that is implemented helps preserve confidence and trust, without which no peace process can prosper in the long term. The DRC's experience in the area of armed conflicts in the Great Lakes region teaches us that when the rules designed to protect people are weakened, it is the civilian population that pays the price. That is why we call upon all parties to put the protection of life and human dignity above immediate political considerations for the Democratic Republic Congo, the recent exchanges show that even amidst this test, dialogue remains possible when there is political will. This reality should be built upon today so that it can steadily lead to a more structured dialogue, a ceasefire and ultimately a lasting cessation of hostilities. It is with this in mind that my delegation will continue to support any initiative in accordance with international law that can bring the parties closer together and help bring about a just negotiated lasting peace in accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter. Thank you.
I thank the representative from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and I give the floor to the representative of Pakistan.

I thank the representative of Pakistan and I give the floor to the representative of Colombia.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Colombia wishes to thank the delegations of Latvia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine for convening this meeting. We also wish to thank the participants and briefers for their invaluable contributions and moving testimony. The protection of persons deprived of freedom during armed conflict is one of the pillars of international humanitarian law. Geneva Conventions establish clear obligations regarding the humane treatment of prisoners of war, civilian detainees and all persons protected under IHL. Colombia reaffirms that compliance with international humanitarian law is an obligation that must be upheld under all circumstances and by all parties. The prohibition of torture and of cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment, as well as the prohibition of forced disappearances and of summary executions are all non-derogable obligations. Distinguished colleagues, Colombia notes with concern the reports detailing alleged violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law concerning persons deprived of freedom. These reports emphasize the need to strengthen prevention, documentation, investigation and accountability. Against this backdrop, my delegation wishes to underscore the vital role played by the International Committee of the Red Cross as a neutral and independent actor. We appeal to all parties to protect and facilitate the committee's access to prisoners of war and to civilian detainees. This in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. This access is vital in order to verify detention conditions, as well as to maintain contact with families and to shed light on the whereabouts of missing persons. Colombia is of the view that it is crucial to devote particular attention to the situation of third country nationals that are involved in or affected by the conflict, they must be examined through a strictly humanitarian and legal lens. Nationality does not automatically determine the legal status of a person, neither can it trigger the denial or curtailment of protections provided for under international humanitarian law and international human rights law. With this in mind, we urge all parties to guarantee, without discrimination on grounds of nationality, the full respect of human rights and of the protections provided for international humanitarian law. These protections include access to humanitarian assistance, to communication with family members and with consular authorities. To conclude, Colombia encourages the continuation of humanitarian efforts and the implementation of measures designed to mitigate the suffering of people affected and their families. Colombia will continue to support efforts designed to increase compliance with international humanitarian law and to guarantee the protection of civilians and of all persons affected by armed conflicts in accordance with the principles of the United Nations Charter. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Colombia for his statement and I will now open the floor to those member states inscribed on the list of speakers and give the floor now to the representative of the European Union.

Thank you, Your Excellencies, dear colleagues, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova and Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia, as well as Andorra, align themselves with this statement. I thank Latvia, the UK, and Ukraine for calling this meeting, and I thank all five briefers for their powerful testimony. Four and a half years into Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine, humanitarian consequences continue to deepen dramatically. According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, in the first six months of 2026, 1,396 civilians have been killed, and 7,978 injured. This is 37% higher than in the same period in 2025 and 114% higher than in 2024. Russia's relentless and escalating large-scale missile and drone attacks, including strikes against targeting residential areas and civilian infrastructure, are tormenting Ukraine daily. Overwhelming evidence demonstrates that Russia continues to violate the Geneva Conventions in total disregard for international humanitarian law. Its widespread and systematic practice of arbitrarily detaining Ukrainian civilians in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine and within the Russian Federation is unacceptable and must be condemned. Civilians have been deprived of their liberty simply for expressing pro-Ukrainian views, carrying out their professional duties, participating in peaceful civic activities, or refusing to cooperate with the occupying authorities. There are credible reports of enforced disappearances, incommunicado detention, torture, sexual violence, denial of due process, and unlawful transfers. Thousands of Ukrainian civilians remain in Russian captivity, while the fate and whereabouts of many others remain unknown. Russia systematically continues to refuse to provide information on detainees to their families and to international humanitarian organisations, prolonging the suffering of relatives. Under international law, families have the right to know the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones. Civilians may only be interned in exceptional circumstances, under the Fourth Geneva Convention and must be released as soon as the reasons necessitating their internment no longer exist. In its report of September 2025, the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Russian Federation, Marianna Katsorova, whose mandate the EU fully supports, drew attention to the widespread and systematic torture and ill treatment in the Russian Federation affecting Russian citizens, Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees by Russian law enforcement officials, security forces, penitentiary officials and members of the armed forces. In the SG's 2025 report on conflict related sexual violence, Russian armed and security forces are listed for the first time for committing conflict-related sexual violence against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in the context of its war of aggression against Ukraine. The European Union reiterates its call for the immediate and unconditional release of all civilians arbitrarily detained by Russia. Pending their release, they must be treated humanely, protected from torture and other ill treatment, and afforded all guarantees provided under international law. We also specifically call on Russia to immediately ensure the safe and unconditional return of all unlawfully deported and transferred Ukrainian children, as also requested by the GA in its resolution of December 2025. The situation of Ukrainian prisoners of war in Russian captivity remains equally alarming. All prisoners of war, without any discrimination, are entitled to the protections of the Third Geneva Convention. Yet the United Nations has consistently documented Russia's widespread and systemic use of torture and other forms of ill-treatment of prisoners of war. Former detainees have described severe beatings, electric shocks, mock executions, prolonged stress positions, sexual violence, denial of adequate food and medical care, and other forms of cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment. Reports of summary executions of captured Ukrainian soldiers have become increasingly frequent and constitute grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, amounting to war crimes. Russia must immediately cease these violations, fully and unconditionally comply with its obligations under international law, and cooperate with international humanitarian actors. The International Committee of the Red Cross must be enabled to fulfil its mandate. It must be ensured that the ICRC has access to all places where Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees are held and contribute to the confirmation of the fate and whereabouts of persons reported missing in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Dear colleagues, the EU also strongly condemns Russia's deceitful recruitment of third country citizens including many from African and Latin American countries, to fight in its illegal and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine and to work in its military industry. Over 3,500 foreign nationals are independently confirmed to have died fighting for Russia. The EU will continue to engage with affected countries and Ukraine on this matter. Furthermore, the EU strongly condemns DPRK-Russia military cooperation, including arms transfers and the deployment of DPRK troops in support of Russia's war of aggression. These activities constitute a serious breach of international law, including the UN Charter, and a flagrant violation of multiple UN Security Council resolutions that Russia itself supported. The DPRK and Russia must immediately cease their illegal military cooperation. The European Union will continue to stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes in pursuit of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law. We reaffirm our commitment to justice and full accountability for international crimes and other violations of international law committed in the context of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. And I thank you.

I thank the representative of Timor-Leste and I will now give the floor to the representative of Estonia.

Thank you, Chair. Estonia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. We thank Latvia, the United Kingdom, together with Ukraine for organising this meeting. We are deeply moved by the harrowing testimonies of the briefers today, especially Ms Umarova and Mr Garcia, thank you for being here. What you have gone through is a testament to courage and endurance, but also a profound tragedy. As we have heard today, Russia's war against Ukraine extends beyond the battlefield. It is waged through captivity, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, and the deportation and forcible transfer of children. These are all tools of repression and control. For 12 years now, since 2014, with the illegal annexation of Crimea and the occupation of parts of Donetsk and Luhansk, a number of credible sources, including the UN mechanisms, have documented systematic torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees in Russian captivity. The reports make it clear that these are not isolated incidents, but systematic practices endorsed by Russian leadership. We urge the Security Council to take due note of these independent reports and their findings and incorporate them into the Council work and considerations. We urge Member States to demand Russia to cease the torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and detainees and support initiatives that help putting a stop to Russia's crimes. Torturing or humiliating a captive is not only cowardly and utterly shameful, It is in clear violation of international humanitarian law and human rights law. They amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity. To this day, thousands of Ukrainians remain unlawfully detained and more than 16,000 civilians from occupied territories are missing. We call on Russia to release all unlawfully detained civilians and disclose the fate and whereabouts of every missing person. Seriously wounded and ill prisoners of war must be repatriated without delay. Prisoner exchanges need to continue. A critical issue that needs to be addressed is Russian denial of access to UN and ICRC representatives to their detention facilities. The ICRC and UN monitors must be granted full, regular and confidential access to all prisoners of war and civilian detainees. Ukraine, on the contrary, has shown that it takes its obligations under international humanitarian law seriously and has granted international monitors unhindered access to its detention facilities. The OHCHR has found conditions that are largely compliant with international standards. Estonia also condemns Russia's exploitation of foreign nationals through deceptive and coercive recruitment practices. This unlawful activity needs to stop. It is important to disrupt these networks and assist the victims. Chair, Russia's actions must be met with accountability. There will be no lasting peace for Ukraine without ensuring accountability for violations of international law committed during Russia's war of aggression. We support the ICC and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine in their mission to find impunity and bring justice to all the victims of this war. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Estonia for her statement. I will now give the floor to the representative of Liechtenstein.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I want to thank you and I want to thank our briefers for their personal bravery and for coming to speak with us today and to express our solidarity with them. Russia's ongoing aggression against Ukraine is shocking not only in its brazen violation of the prohibition of the illegal use of force, but also as the latest chapter in a consistent approach to international law, which disregards the basic tenets of international humanitarian law in a systematic way, amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity. By all of its own metrics, Russia's aggression has failed. It has failed to topple the democratically elected government of Ukraine, failed to break the spirit of the Ukrainian people, and failed to divide the support in Europe for international law. But as it fails in Ukraine, its crimes against Ukrainians, including prisoners of war, civilian detainees, and foreign fighters, have only worsened. Lichtenstein notes that most of the Ukrainian victims of conflict related sexual violence are men and boys subjected to sexual torture, rape and other forms of violence during imprisonment. Based on the verified information available, the perpetrators of these crimes Russian armed and security forces were listed for the first time as conflict parties credibly suspected of using violence in situations of armed conflict in a systematic manner. Many survivors of such violence face profound stigma that discourages reporting and limits access to specialized support. In this regard, We commend the pioneering work of the Liechtenstein-based All Survivors Project Foundation dedicated to the issue of conflict-related sexual violence against men and boys. In cooperation with partner organizations across Ukraine, it has helped to ensure that survivors can access the necessary support services, including health providers and the justice system. Madam Chair, the International Criminal Court has issued six arrest warrants against Russian nationals for alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes in Ukraine. The court, of course, cannot deliver results alone. The execution of arrest warrants is indispensable, and we look to all states parties to fulfill their legal obligations under the Rome Statute. The case of Ukraine highlights that the court is not a threat to state sovereignty, but rather an expression of it, as Ukraine made the sovereign decision to submit itself to the court's jurisdiction. By doing so, it sent a clear message that no crimes committed by its nationals or on its soil will remain unpunished while it continues to prioritize its own exercise of jurisdiction. Madam Chair, the resolutions adopted in this building since 2022, in particular the Just Peace resolution adopted by the General Assembly, must be the basis for any meaningful initiative for peace in Ukraine. We look forward to an end to a war that has caused immense suffering to the civilian population, created economic damages amounting to hundreds of billions of dollars, and destroyed the European security architecture. To ensure accountability under international law, including for the crime of aggression, to bring justice to all victims and survivors, and lasting peace to all of Europe. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Liechtenstein for his statement, and I will now give the floor to the representative of Albania.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Albania aligned with European Union statements, but I would like to have some remarks in my national capacity. I would like to thank Latvia, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine for convening this meeting. We also thank the briefers for their valuable insights, which have highlighted the profound human consequences of the war in Ukraine and the urgent need to protect those affected by it. More than four years after the beginning of Russia's full-scale aggression against Ukraine, the humanitarian consequences remain deeply concerning. Behind the figures, reports, and testimonies presented today are people whose lives have been profoundly affected, including prisoners of war, civilian detainees, and their families. International humanitarian law provides essential protection to people affected by armed conflict. The Geneva Convention and their additional protocols, as applicable, as well as customary international humanitarian law must be fully respected. We are concerned by reports of torture, ill treatment, arbitrary detention, and other serious violations affecting prisoners of war and civilian detainees. The consistent accounts of torture and ill-treatment reported by international human rights mechanisms are particularly alarming. These allegations must not go unanswered. They must be properly documented and investigated, and those responsible for violation must be held accountable in accordance with international law. We therefore stress the importance of regular, safe and unhindered access by the International Committee of the Red Cross to all prisoners of war and civilian detainees in accordance with its mandate. Access is not a humanitarian concession. It is an essential safeguard for the protection of persons deprived of their liberty. Families must receive timely and reliable information concerning the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones. Humanitarian concerns must never become instruments of pressure or bargaining, and the dignity of those deprived of their liberty must be respected at all times. Colleagues, We are also deeply concerned by reports of the deceptive and coercive recruitment of foreign nationals into the Russian armed forces. The reported use of promises of civilian employment, recruitment networks and online platforms to target vulnerable individuals followed by pressure to sign military contracts they may not understand raises serious concerns regarding exploitation and coercion. The recruitment and deployment of foreign nationals through deceptive or coercive practices must not be allowed to become another dimension of human exploiting arising from this war. Madam Chair, the United Nations has an important role to play in reinforcing respect for international humanitarian law. The Security Council must continue to uphold the principles reached in the United Nations Charter and insist on compliance with applicable international humanitarian law. Existing international mechanisms should be supported and strengthened, including through systematic documentation, monitoring and reporting of violations. At the critical juncture, our collective responsibility is clear, to uphold the charter of the United Nation and international law, to protect civilians and all persons deprived of their liberty, to ensure humanitarian access, to facilitate exchanges and returns, and strengthen accountability for serious violations. I thank you.

I thank the representative of Albania for her statement and I will kindly ask all the speakers to keep their remarks concise so that we can hear all the Member States inscribed on the list of speakers. And I will now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I'd like to thank Latvia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine for convening today's meeting. I also thank the briefers for their insightful remarks. Since the beginning of Russia's aggression against Ukraine, we have continued to see clear and blatant violations of international law, including the UN Charter, alongside reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. Japan emphasizes the importance of principled view that attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force are unlawful and must not be tolerated. Japan also expresses its strong condemnations of Russia's widespread and systematic use of torture against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war, including sexual violence as a form of torture. Japan calls for humane and dignified treatment of all Ukrainian POWs and civilian detainees in Russian custody. General Assembly resolution 80/223 urges Russia to uphold the rights of Ukrainian prisoners and detainees, including securing appropriate conditions for POWs in accordance with Geneva Convention. Further, Russia must provide reliable information on the whereabouts of detained Ukrainian civilians, including POWs, and release all residents of the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories who have been unlawfully arrested or detained. Yet these requirements remain almost entirely unimplemented. Japan is also concerned by the reports of coercive and deceptive recruitment of foreign nationals into Russian armed forces, as mentioned in the 2026 report of Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine. Additionally, we are deeply concerned by the continued deployment of North Korean soldiers in combat against Ukraine, which constitutes a clear violation of international law. including the UN Charter and Security Council resolutions. Such unlawful military cooperation between Russia and DPRK is undermining peace and security in Europe, the Indo-Pacific, and beyond. Madam Chair, human rights apply to all persons, including POWs and civilian detainees, and peace processes must respect human life and dignity. Japan will continue to stand with the people of Ukraine and work alongside the international community towards a just and lasting peace. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Japan for his statement. I will now give the floor to the representative of Switzerland.

Madam Chair, Switzerland thanks the organisers of this meeting and the briefers for their briefings. We continue to strongly condemn Russia's war against Ukraine. We consider it to be a grave violation of international law. We call for an immediate cessation of all hostilities and once again urge Russia to withdraw its troops from Ukraine. Allow me to highlight three points. First, international humanitarian law must be strictly respected by all parties. We are alarmed by reports of violations. Such violations must be investigated and those responsible, whoever they may be, must be brought to justice. International humanitarian law requires the protection of civilians and of civilian objects. Rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access must be ensured. All attacks targeting civilians or civilian objects, including missile strikes, are prohibited and must cease immediately. Second, prisoners of war and other detainees and internees must be protected and treated humanely. All captured persons must be protected at all times, namely against violence, intimidation, insults and public curiosity. As an impartial humanitarian actor and pursuant to its unique mandate under the Geneva Conventions, the International Committee of the Red Cross must be granted access to all prisoners of war and internees. This access is vital for monitoring detention conditions, facilitating contact with families and promoting compliance with international humanitarian law. We call upon all parties to provide the RCRC with full access. Switzerland remains ready to offer its good offices, including in support of humanitarian efforts. That readiness was demonstrated by its facilitation of the talks that led to a prisoner exchange last March. My third point now, respect for international law is vital to achieving a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. Switzerland remains staunchly committed to such a peace based on the UN Charter and the Helsinki Principles. This is one of the priorities of its chairpersonship of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security rests with the Security Council. Consequently, we call upon all parties to work towards a just and lasting peace. Thank you.

We continue to call for the Russian Federation to be held to account for these reported violations and we stand firmly with Ukraine and call on Russia to end this senseless war.
