I thank the representative of Australia for his remarks and I will now give the floor to the representative of Georgia.

Thank you, Madam Chair. At the outset, let me thank Latvia and the United Kingdom and Ukraine for convening today's important meeting. I also thank briefers for their important contributions. We welcome this discussion on the implementation of international humanitarian law, particularly regarding the protection of prisoners of war and civilian detainees. Respect for international humanitarian law is not optional. Even in times of war, the Geneva Conventions establish clear obligations to protect human dignity, prohibit torture and ill-treatment and ensure human treatment of all persons deprived of their liberty. Georgia remains deeply concerned by continued reports documenting systematic torture and ill-treatment, arbitrary detention and forced disappearances, conflict-related sexual violence, summary executions and other serious violations committed against Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees held in the custody of the Russian Federation. Such acts continue grave breaches of international humanitarian law and violations of international human rights law and must be subject to prompt, thorough and independent investigations, as well as full accountability for those responsible. Madam Chair, as we marked just days ago the 18 years since the beginning of Russia's war against Georgia, this discussion carries particular significance for my country. Georgia knows firsthand the human cost of armed conflict and illegal occupation. This experience has also been confirmed by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights and the International Criminal Court. The recent judgment of the European Court of Human Rights concerning the torture and killing of the Georgian prisoners of war during the 2008 war, including Georgia's national hero, Georgy Dzhokharidze, as well as the decision of the International Criminal Court, which led to the issuance of International Criminal Court of arrest warrants for war crimes committed against ethnic Georgians, once again underscores the importance of ensuring accountability for serious violations of international humanitarian law. For years, international monitoring mechanisms have continued to be denied access to Russia occupied regions of Georgia, Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, while the security, human rights and humanitarian situations on the ground remains deeply alarming. Our experience demonstrates that where international humanitarian and human rights law is disregarded and independent monitoring is obstructed, violations become deeply rooted. Impunity deepens and the suffering of victims is prolonged. Madam Chair, Georgia supports all efforts aimed at securing the release and safe return of prisoners of war and unlawfully detained civilians. Every change represents not merely a humanitarian achievement but also a reaffirmation that international humanitarian law must remain at the center of efforts to alleviate the human cost of armed conflict. The international community must remain united and resolute. Attempts to redraw internationally recognized borders by force must never be tolerated. We therefore call on Russia to fully comply with its obligations under the UN Charter and international law, including its obligations under international humanitarian law, ensure unhindered access for impartial humanitarian organizations to facilitate the return of prisoners of war and unlawfully detained civilians, and ensure credible investigations into all alleged violations. Georgia reaffirms its unwavering support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders and for upholding a rules-based international order grounded in the UN Charter and accountability for violations of international law. I thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the representative of Georgia for his statement and I will now give the floor to the representative of Finland.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I have the honour of delivering this statement on behalf of the Nordic countries, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and my own country, Finland. Almost four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we continue to witness Russia's systematic and gross violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights. According to the OHCHR Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, nearly all Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed after release from Russian captivity reported regular torture, ill treatment or abuse. We are particularly alarmed by the reports of the extrajudicial killings which may amount to a war crime. Russia's use of so-called filtration procedures in occupied territories has led to detention of civilians perceived as loyal to Ukraine, including journalists, local leaders and relatives of Ukrainian service members. The Nordics are deeply concerned by reports that foreign nationals have been recruited into the Russian armed forces through deceptive and coercive practices. These findings underscore the global repercussions of Russia's war of aggression. The Nordic countries strongly condemn Russia's war of aggression and call on Russia to uphold its obligations the international humanitarian law, including by treating detainees humanely and with dignity and granting the ICRC immediate and unimpeded access to all Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees. Arbitrary detention, inhumane treatment and enforced disappearance are violations of international law and may amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity. The Nordic countries remain deeply concerned by reports of conflict-related sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees in Russian captivity. We commend Ukraine's efforts to establish survivor-centred CRSV referral mechanisms and to develop expertise in the investigation and prosecution of war crimes. We reaffirm our support to Ukrainian investigators, the International Criminal Court, reparation mechanisms and civil society documentation to ensure full accountability in the context of Russian aggression. The international community should ensure that these lessons are incorporated into accountability processes beyond Ukraine. The Nordic countries strongly support the global initiative to galvanise political commitment to international humanitarian law and its call to use IHL as a guiding framework to reduce suffering and help steer armed conflicts towards peaceful resolution. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Finland for her statement. I will now give the floor to the representative of Lithuania.

Thank you, Madam President. Lithuania aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the European Union. Lithuania extends its sincere gratitude to Latvia, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine for convening this important Area Four Molar meeting, and thanks all briefers, particularly those who shared their personal testimonies. The accounts are a vivid reminder of the human cost of Russia's illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine and the urgent need to uphold international humanitarian law. The findings of the OHCHR, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine and OSCE confirm widespread and systematic violations, including torture, arbitrary detention, conflict-related sexual violence, denial of medical care and executions of prisoners of war. The Commission of Inquiry has concluded that torture committed by Russian authorities amount to a crime against humanity. These violations demand accountability. The gravity of these violations is reflected in UN reporting. In 2026, Russian armed forces were listed once again by the UN Secretary General for grave violations, including for the first time in relation to conflict-related sexual violence, with repeated listings carrying consequences for participation in UN peacekeeping operations. The international community must demand full compliance with the Geneva Conventions, Russia must immediately grant the ICRC the unhindered access to all prisoners of war and civilian detainees provided for under the Third and Fourth Geneva Conventions, allow access for all relevant human rights mechanisms, including the Special Rapporteur on Torture, and fully implement the Mandela Rules, ensuring humane treatment, adequate medical care, and family contacts, as required under international law. Lithuania welcomes humanitarian efforts to alleviate suffering, including prisoner exchanges, especially those seriously wounded and sick. We would also support strengthening of rehabilitation programs for released prisoners of war and civilian detainees through enhanced cooperation with the UN, WHO, and humanitarian organizations. Let me conclude by reiterating Lithuania's unwavering support for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. Russia must stop its brutal aggression immediately, withdraw its forces from the sovereign territory of Ukraine, comply fully with its obligation under the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and international human rights law and ensure the immediate protection of all prisoners of war and civilian detainees. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Lithuania for his statement and I will now give the floor to the representative of Spain.

Thank you. Spain joins in thanking Latvia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine for convening this meeting. We also align with the statement of the European Union and I will make some comments in addition in my national capacity. Russia's systematic attacks against the civilian population and critical infrastructure of Ukraine constitute violations of international humanitarian law and must cease immediately. Spain most firmly condemns continued violations by Russia of human rights and international humanitarian law in Ukraine through summary executions of prisoners of war and detained civilians, arbitrary detentions, the systematic and widespread use of torture and other forms of ill treatment. The Office of the High Commissioner recently reported new executions of Ukrainian prisoners and that almost all of Ukrainian prisoners of war that have been released that were then interviewed reported having suffered torture or mistreatment. Prisoners of war must receive humane treatment at all times. Russia must guarantee the International Committee of the Red Cross full, regular, unhindered access to all prisoners of war and civilian internees and to all places of detention. And this is a point that many delegations throughout this meeting have reiterated. Their families have the right to know their fate and their whereabouts. The ICRC itself has said that it still lacks full access to all of them. We express profound concern over the rising number of civilians killed and injured due to Russia's use of mass drone and ballistic missile attacks in residential and urban areas. Spain also joins the call for the immediate and unconditional release of all prisoners of war and civilians that have been arbitrarily detained by Russia. Moreover, we specifically call upon Russia to immediately guarantee the safe and unconditional return of all Ukrainian children that have been illegally deported and moved. Russia must immediately cease these violations. It must fully comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law and must cooperate with international humanitarian actors. No argument can justify a war of aggression which each day leads to more civilian casualties, the systematic destruction of essential infrastructure and a humanitarian crisis of global proportions. Russia is directly challenging the principles of sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity. Deliberate attacks against the civilian population are war crimes, and they should be unequivocally described as such. Equally, violations committed in the occupied territories are crimes that cannot go unpunished. Our message is firm and unambiguous. Russia must immediately cease its aggression and withdraw all of its troops from the territory of Ukraine to within its internationally recognized borders. Only then will it be possible to pave the way towards a just and lasting peace rooted in the United Nations Charter and the principles and values of international law. In the meantime, Spain will continue to actively assist Ukraine. In response to the humanitarian crisis caused by Russia's aggression against Ukraine, Spain has launched a humanitarian assistance package that is without precedent in the history of our cooperation, with more than 120 million allocated since February 2022. Spain will continue to support all diplomatic efforts aimed at achieving peace, while we will also maintain our political, financial, humanitarian and security contribution to support Ukraine's sovereignty and right to defend itself. A lasting peace also requires accountability. We reiterate our commitment to accountability for international crimes committed in the context of this war of aggression. Therefore, we fully support the establishment of accountability mechanisms that should begin operating as soon as possible. That is the main way to demand accountability from Russia and to respond to the crimes committed and the damage that has been caused. Spain urges all members of the United Nations to support the instruments for the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine and the claims commission. My country supports efforts aimed at bringing those responsible to justice and to restoring peace and stability in Ukraine in accordance with international law and in particular with the United Nations Charter. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Spain for his statement and I will now give the floor to the representative of Germany.

Madam Chair, thank you for, thank you co-conveners for convening this important meeting today. I also thank the Secretariat for its insightful briefing and I extend my special.

And sincere gratitude to Mrs. Umarova and Mr. Garcia for their extraordinary courage in testifying about the terrible experiences endured.

In countless reports, independent bodies of the United Nations have detailed Russia's grave violations of international humanitarian and human rights.

Law.

Russia's violations of international humanitarian law in its unprovoked, unjustified, and illegal war of aggression against Ukraine are well documented. It is not enough to simply repeat calls to both parties of the armed conflict. Violations must be registered, perpetrators must be held accountable. To uphold international humanitarian law, it must be made clear that states that do not comply with their obligations will face real consequences.

Ukraine grants the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross unfettered access to prisoners of war.

The sheer scale and frequency of their reported activities in Ukraine clearly demonstrate that they can operate and visit detainees.

Freely.

This stands in stark contrast to Russia. which does not grant free unhindered access to independent monitors. Rather, Russia continues to systematically block independent monitors. The profound discrepancy in what international bodies are able to verify and report on speaks for itself.

We call on all member states to clearly state their expectation.

Russia must comply with international humanitarian law, including in its treatment of prisoners of war.

This means granting immediate, unimpeded and repeated access to all Ukrainian prisoners of war. The systematic ill-treatment and torture of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees must stop now. The role of the ICRC regarding prisoners of war, civilian internees and other persons deprived of their liberties is of paramount importance. As a strategic partner and top financial contributor to the ICRC, we extend our deepest respect and gratitude for its tireless dedication to fulfilling its vital mandate under the Geneva Conventions.

Madam Chair, on every level Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has inflicted immeasurable human suffering, reaching far beyond the European continent.

Russia's illegal practice of luring and coercing foreign nationals into its military exploits vulnerable individuals.

And brings profound loss to families across Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

This apparent war must end.

Every single member of the Security Council, with the sole exception of Russia, has echoed the Secretary-General's call for ceasefire. Ukraine has repeatedly stated that it stands ready to agree to such a ceasefire immediately. We urge all member states to help make Russia's leadership understand that the only responsible choice, both ethically and politically, is to pursue that same track.

I thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Germany for his statement and I will now give the floor to the representative of Poland.

Madam Chair, I would like to thank the Permanent Missions of Latvia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine for convening today's meeting and for drawing attention to the grave violations committed by Russia in the course of its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. I also thank the briefers for their deeply moving testimonies. There is no legal vacuum in armed conflict. Every prisoner of war and every civilian detainee is protected under international law. Russia is fully bound by these obligations and yet it continues to deliberately and systematically violate international humanitarian law. The evidence is overwhelming. According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, more than 96% of interviewed Ukrainian prisoners of war reported being subjected to torture or other forms of ill treatment. 96%. Additionally, since February 2022, the executions of at least 1929 Ukrainian prisoners of war have been documented. Furthermore, Russia denies fair trial guarantees to Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilians. The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has documented the use of fabricated evidence, confessions extracted under torture, and politically motivated prosecutions. Prosecuting prisoners of war merely for the lawful participation in hostilities has no basis in international humanitarian law. Poland calls for the release of all persons convicted on such unlawful grounds. Madam Chair, humanitarian access remains essential. We call on Russia to provide meaningful, immediate, and unimpeded access to all places of detention for the International Committee of the Red Cross and other independent international monitoring mechanisms. Russia must disclose the identity and whereabouts of all persons in its custody and ensure regular communication between detainees and their families. Compliance with international humanitarian law is not a matter for negotiation. We are also deeply concerned by Russia's increasing reliance on the recruitment of foreign nationals to sustain its war against Ukraine. These practices raise serious concerns regarding exploitation, coercion, and trafficking in persons. This recruitment is often facilitated through disinformation and information manipulation campaigns targeting vulnerable individuals in many parts of the world. Often recruits are lured by false promises of civilian employment only to find themselves deceived into military service. Those refusing to fight made themselves become victims of torture or other abuse. Their families are often denied reliable information about their fate, promised salaries frequently do not materialize, And in many cases, the bodies of those killed are not returned. This is Russia's way of waging war, showing complete disregard not only for human life, but also for the citizens of third countries whom it exploits for its military purposes. We therefore call on governments whose nationals may be targeted to strengthen information sharing, counter Russian disinformation, investigate deceptive recruitment networks, and take concrete measures to protect vulnerable individuals from exploitation. I thank you.

I thank the representative of Poland for his statement. A little remark, we still have three Member States inscribed on the list and five minutes left. I understand the interpreters are ready to stay a few more minutes, so I suggest that we take the three speakers inscribed with the interpreters and then we will release the interpreters and we can stay a few more minutes to conclude this meeting. So I will now give the floor to the representative of Romania.

Madam President, Romania aligns with the statement delivered by the European Union and we join others in thanking Latvia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine for organising this meeting. We also thank our briefers for their substantial and moving accounts. Russia's illegal and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine constitutes a complete disregard for the UN Charter and the rules, norms, and principles of international law, including international humanitarian law. This conduct is particularly grave. First, because it is conducted by a permanent member of the UN Security Council, an organ of the United Nations to which all states have entrusted a primary role for peace and security. Second, because equal disregard is manifested towards the way the war is waged. The evidence is stark, and it is highlighted by several UN mechanisms, including the Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, the Special Rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in the Russian Federation, the Secretary-General's reports on thematic areas of concern on the Council's agenda, as well as by the humanitarian organizations, by open source evidence, and through the accounts of victims themselves. enforced restrictions on fundamental rights in occupied territories, arbitrary and incommunicado detentions of civilians, enforced disappearances, denial of due process and unlawful transfers, including, as we know, of children, refusal to provide information on detainees to families and international humanitarian organizations about the fate and whereabouts of loved ones, denial of adequate food and medical care, conflict-related sexual violence, and other forms of torture, cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment of prisoners, as well as summary executions. This picture reflects widespread and systematic practices in complete violation of the Geneva Conventions and a complete and deliberate disregard of international humanitarian law. As a country with the longest terrestrial border with Ukraine, we have constantly informed the Security Council of the millions of Ukrainians which have crossed the Romanian border in search of safety, as well as of our efforts in support of refugees which choose to remain in our country. We want to also note that behind these statistics, we see and we resonate with the human stories. An overwhelming amount of these stories portray trauma, fear, and separation from family members detained or reported missing. Oftentimes, they refer to leaving for months or years without information about the fate of loved ones. We know and understand directly that these violations, whether they target civilians or prisoners of war, leave a long-lasting mark on those affected, on their families and their communities. They will and must remain a part of historical record. It is essential they are documented, investigated, and prosecuted to address impunity and deter further proliferation of such inhumane behavior. Accountability is and will remain indispensable. Madam President, we reiterate the importance of granting safe, sustained, and unimpeded access to all places of detention for impartial humanitarian organizations. Transparency and independent monitoring are essential safeguards against abuse and mistreatment. We also recall that regardless of nationality, all persons deprived of their liberty in connection with the armed conflict are entitled to humane treatment and the fundamental guarantees provided by international law. We welcome and call for the continuation of prisoner exchanges, as well as for the unconditional release of unlawfully detained civilians. As a member of the International Coalition for the Return of the Ukrainian Children, Romania supports all efforts aimed at the implementation of the General Assembly resolution on the topic to ensure full accountability for these crimes committed by the Russian Federation. The return of Ukrainian children remains central to any effort towards a dignified and durable peace and constitutes a matter of principle. Finally, we reiterate our support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, and we call for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace anchored in international law and the principles of the UN Charter. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Romania for her statement, and I will now give the floor to the representative of Czech Republic.

Thank you, Madam President.

The Czech Republic reaffirms its unwavering support for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity. We welcome the release of Mrs. Umerova and Mr. Garcia, who join us today. Yet their freedom also reminds us of thousands of Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war who remain in Russian captivity or are deprived of their liberty in temporarily occupied territories. including those held on fabricated charges and denied their fundamental rights. Many are subjected to torture, ill treatment and enforced disappearances. Families are left without information, while victims are left without protection.

These.

Grave violations of international humanitarian law, documented by the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, must not go unpunished. Russia must grant regular and unimpeded access to all detainees, including for the ICRC and other international relevant organizations. It is a matter of profound concern that Russia, which helped shape the post-war international legal order and remains bound by the Geneva Conventions, is disregarding the very principles it once helped establish.

Documenting these crimes is the first step towards justice. The Czech Republic works closely with civil society.

Organizations and human rights defenders who preserve evidence for future accountability and document abuses that Russia seeks to conceal. The deceptive recruitment of foreign nationals is yet another manifestation of Russia's disregard for international norms. Those who exploit vulnerable individuals, organise or knowingly tolerate these schemes must be held accountable. Madam President, human lives must remain at the centre of all peace efforts. Efforts to facilitate the exchange of prisoners of war and return of unlawfully detained civilians should therefore remain a priority. The protection and return of prisoners of war and the release of unlawfully detained civilians must form an essential part of any credible path towards a just and lasting peace.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of the Czech Republic for his statement and I will now give the floor to the last speaker on my list, the United Arab Emirates.

Madam President, allow me to thank Latvia for convening today's meeting and I thank all the briefers for their valuable insights. The UAE remains deeply concerned by the continued human suffering caused by the conflict in Ukraine. After more than four years of conflict, the need to protect civilians and address humanitarian needs is as urgent as ever. We reiterate our call on all parties to uphold their obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law. Madam President, we have seen that even amid the most difficult circumstances, There remain opportunities to bridge divides and produce tangible humanitarian outcomes. In this regard, we thank both the Russian Federation and Ukraine for the trust they have placed in the UAE's mediation efforts, which to date have resulted in 25 exchange operations of prisoners of wars and the release of 7,791 prisoners. These exchanges were made possible by the cooperation and goodwill of both the Russian Federation and Ukraine, and we will continue to place our good offices at the service of both parties. Madam President, we reaffirm the importance of inclusive dialogue and sustained political engagement towards a peaceful settlement of the conflict. We welcome and encourage all diplomatic efforts in this regard, and we are convinced that the same spirit of cooperation that has enabled successive prisoner exchanges can help build confidence towards broader de-escalation and ultimately a durable peace. In conclusion, The UAE will continue to support all serious efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace in the region. Thank you, Madam President.

I thank the representative of the United Arab Emirates for his statement. As we only have the conclusion remaining, I'm happy to thank the interpreters for staying a little over time and release them. and we will now proceed to the end of this meeting. Before we do that, I see that the Russian Federation has requested the floor. So the Chair will give the floor to the Russian Federation for a final intervention, and I would encourage the delegation to be brief and focused and keep the intervention within one or two minutes, so that, especially because all the main points have already been extensively heard, and we would encourage bringing this discussion to a close without further complications. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Madam Coordinator, for giving me the floor again. I just wanted to bring a couple of facts that may be helpful for the understanding of the situation. So first of all, I wanted to highlight that the only source of information that is being voiced, you know, we say about many reports within the UN framework and outside. But the only source of information for all those reports is actually the Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. So this mission have never been mandated by anybody to collect evidence. It stays in Ukraine on the bilateral agreement with Kiev. And actually, it works under the control of the government. And also, it works for the benefit of its sponsors. And I wanted to highlight the contribution of a number of states to that mission. So for instance, Canada contributes 1 million, Germany, 3 millions, Ireland, 700,000, Netherlands, 5 millions, Norway, 1 million, Sweden, 1 and 1/2 million, Switzerland, 1 million, UK, 1 million. So you see that this particular mission is financed by exactly those countries who are taking the floor today. And also, by the way of conclusion, I wanted to highlight that those countries are actually extensively providing weapons that are now being used by Ukraine against Russia and Russian civilians. And you probably don't know that Canada provided 6.5 billion dollars of military assistance. Germany, tens of billions. Netherlands, nine billion. Norway, 1.3 billion. Sweden, 11 billion. United Kingdom, more than 13 billion. Denmark, 4.4 billion. France, six billion of military assistance and also equipment. And just my last statement concerns the ICC that was mentioned here. It is very interesting that this institution, which loses its members, its participants, and also its prosecutor is somehow mentioned here as a worthy institution. But by coincidence, Ukraine somehow does not trust it because when they joined the Rome Statute of the ICC, they made the reservation to that statute. actually taking off the jurisdiction on war crimes. So it's exempted itself for the war crimes jurisdiction of the ICC for seven years. So I was wondering if this is such a good institution and the Ukraine puts a lot of trust in it, probably should withdraw this reservation and enjoy the full capacity of the services of the ICC. And I thank you.
I thank the Russian Federation. I will now give the floor to my co-chair for some final remarks.

Thanks very much. And particularly thank you to our briefers today for their powerful and deeply moving testimony. Your accounts have underscored the human cost of this war far beyond the battlefield and put, names and faces to the stories of many others. The United Kingdom will continue to provide vital support to Ukraine, including training for Ukrainian personnel, actions that are in full respect of international law, including international humanitarian law. Ultimately, the only way to end this suffering is to end the war itself. We need an immediate ceasefire and a just and lasting settlement now so that prisoners can return home, families can begin to heal, and Ukraine can move towards a secure and peaceful future. Thank you.

Thank you. And a few words from my side as well. Dear colleagues, I wish to thank you all for your participation and for your statements. And I also, and in particular, would like to warmly thank all our briefers. And say that the courage and the presence of Ms. Omerova and Mr. Garcia here are a reminder that the spirit of Ukraine cannot be broken and will not be broken. And we also do reiterate our call for an immediate, full, and unconditional ceasefire. Latvia stands with Ukraine and its people fighting for their freedom and for the country's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. And with this, I will conclude this conversation, and let us stand together for the UN Charter and the international humanitarian law, and it's time that this Council acts. I thank you.
